IX. *He is therefore the Author of nature; nor can anything be, or be done, but what He either causes (immediately or mediately) or permits.* All beings (by the last) depend upon Him for their existence; upon whom depends their existence, upon him also must depend the intrinsic manner of their existence, or the *natures* of these beings; and again, upon whom depend their being and nature, upon Him depend the *necessary effects* and *consequences* of their being, and being such as they are in themselves. Then, as to the acts of such of them as may be free agents, and the effects of them, He is indeed *not* the Author of those, because, by the terms and supposition, they proceed from agents who have no necessity imposed upon them by Him to act either this or that way. But yet however these *free agents* must depend upon Him *as such*: from Him they derive their power of acting, and it is He who permits them to use their liberty, though many times, through their own fault, they use it amiss. And, lastly, as to the nature of those relations which lie between ideas or things really existing, or which arise from facts already done and past, these result from the natures of the things themselves﻿—all which the Supreme being either causes or permits (as before). For since things can be but in one manner at once, and their mutual relations, ratios, agreements, disagreements, etc. are nothing but their manners of being with respect to each other, the natures of these relations will be determined by the natures of the things.

===Chinese===

九、*祂因此是自然的创造者；凡事之存在或发生，非祂所（直接或间接地）造成，即祂所容许。*一切存在者（依前一命题）的存在皆系于祂；其存在所系者，其存在的内在方式、即这些存在者的*本性*也必系于祂；再者，其存在与本性所系者，其存在的、其如其所是的存在之*必然效果*与*后果*亦系于祂。至于其中那些自由能动者的行为及其效果，祂诚然*不是*那些行为的作者，因为按字面与假设，它们出自未被祂强加以任何必然、可任意行动的能动者。然而这些*自由的能动者*作为自由能动者仍必系于祂：他们行动的能力得自于祂，是祂容许他们运用其自由，尽管他们常常因自己的过错而滥用。最后，至于存在于观念或实存事物之间的关系、或由既成事实产生的关系的本性，这些皆由事物自身的本性而来——而这一切，至高存在者或造成之、或容许之（如前所述）。因为事物在同一时刻只能以一个方式存在，它们彼此的关系、比例、相合相违等等，无非是它们彼此相对的存在方式，故这些关系的本性将由事物的本性决定。

===Original===

From hence, now it appears that whatever expresses the existences or nonexistences of things, and their mutual relations as they are, is true by the constitution of nature; and if so, it must also be agreeable to His perfect *comprehension* of all truth, and to His *will*, who is at the head of it. Though the act of A (some free agent) is the effect of his liberty, and can only be said to be *permitted* by the Supreme being; yet when it is once done, the relation between the doer and the deed, the agreement there is between A and the idea of one who has committed such a fact, is a fixed relation. From thenceforward it will always be predicable of him, that he was the doer of it: and if anyone should deny this, he would go counter to nature and that great Author of it, whole existence is now proved. And thus those arguments in section I, proposition IV which turned only upon a *supposition* that there was such a Being, are here confirmed and made absolute.

X. *The one supreme and perfect Being, upon whom the existence of all other beings and their powers originally depend, is that Being whom I mean by the word “God.”*

There are other truths still remaining in relation to the Deity, which we may know, and which are necessary to be known by us, if we would endeavor to demean ourselves toward Him according to truth and what He is. And, they are such as not only tend to rectify our opinions concerning His nature and attributes, but also may serve at the same time as further proof of His existence, and an amplification of some things touched perhaps too lightly. As,

XI. *God cannot be corporeal:* or, *there can be no corporeity in God.* There are many things in matter utterly inconsistent with the nature of such a Being as it has been demonstrated God must be.

Matter exists in parts, every one of which, by the term, is imperfect;198 but in a Being absolutely perfect, there can be nothing that is imperfect.

===Chinese===

由此可知，凡如实表达事物之存在或不存在、及其相互关系的，皆因自然之构造而为真；若然，它也必与祂对一切真理的完满*领悟*相合，与居其首位的祂的*意志*相合。虽然 A（某个自由能动者）的行为是其自由的效果，只能说为至高存在者所*容许*；但它一旦做出，行为者与行为之间的关系、A 与「曾犯此事者」的观念之间的相合，便是一种固定的关系。从此以后，「他是做这事的人」将永远可以断言于他；谁若否认这一点，谁就违逆了自然及其伟大的主宰——祂的存在现已被证明。这样，第一节命题四中那些仅依据*假设*——假设有这样一个存在者——的论证，在此得到确认并成为绝对的。

十、*那一位至高而完善的存在者——其余一切存在者及其能力的存在原本系于祂——便是我以「上帝」一词所指的存在者。*

关于神性还有另一些真理为我们可知、也须知，倘若我们愿按真理与祂之所是来对待祂。这些真理不仅能纠正我们关于祂的本性与属性的见解，同时还可以进一步证明祂的存在，并把或许触及得太轻的某些地方加以引申。如：

十一、*上帝不能是有形体的：*或者说，*上帝之中不能有形体性。*物质中有许多东西，与已被证明上帝必是的那样的存在者之本性全然不容。

物质存在于部分之中，而每一部分（就字面而言）都是不完善的；198而在绝对完善的存在者之中，不能有任何不完善之物。

===Original===

These parts, though they are many times kept closely united by some occult influence, are in truth so many distinct bodies, which may, at least in our imagination, be disjoined or placed otherwise; nor can we have any idea of matter, which does not imply a natural discerpibility and susceptivity of various shapes and modifications: i.e. mutability seems to be essential to it. But God, existing in a manner that is perfect, exists in a manner that must be uniform, always one and the same, and in nature unchangeable.

Matter is incapable of acting, passive only, and stupid: which are defects that can never be ascribed to him who is the First cause or Prime agent, the Supreme intellect, and altogether perfect.

Then, if He is corporeal, wherever there is a vacuum, He must be excluded, and so becomes a being bounded, finite, and, as it were, full of chasms.

Lastly, there is no matter or body which may not be *supposed not to be*; whereas the idea of God, or that Being upon whom all others depend, involves in it existence.

XII. *Neither infinite space, nor infinite duration, nor matter infinitely extended or eternally existing, nor any, nor all of these taken together, can be God.*199 For,

Space, taken separately from the things which possess and fill it, is but an empty scene or vacuum; and to say that infinite space is God, or that God is infinite space, is to say that He is an infinite vacuum, than which nothing can be more absurd or blasphemous. How can space, which is but a vast void, rather the negation of all things than positively anything, a kind of diffused nothing; how can this, I say, be the First cause, etc. or indeed any cause? What attributes besides penetrability and extension, what excellencies, what perfections is it capable of?200

As infinite space cannot be God, though He be excluded from no place or space; so, though He is eternal, yet eternity or infinite duration itself is not God.201 For duration, abstracted from all durables, is nothing actually existing by itself: it is the duration of a being, not a being.

Infinite space and duration, taken together, cannot be God: because an interminable space of infinite duration is still nothing but eternal space, and that is at most but an eternal vacuum.

===Chinese===

这些部分虽然常被某种隐秘的影响紧紧连在一起，实际上却是许多各别的物体，至少在我们的想象中可以被拆开或另行安置；我们对物质不可能有任何不包含可分性、可承受各种形状与样态之能力的观念：也就是说，可变性似乎是其本质所固有。而上帝既以完善的方式存在，便是以必然齐一、永远同一、本性不变的方式存在。

物质不能行动，只是被动的、麻木的：这些缺陷决不能归之于那作为第一因或元动者、至高的理智、全然完善者。

再者，祂若是有形的，则凡有真空之处祂必被排除在外，于是成为一个有界、有限、仿佛处处罅隙的存在者。

最后，任何物质或物体无不可以被*设想为不存在*；而上帝——即那万物所系的存在者——的观念则包含着存在。

十二、*无论无限的空间、无限的绵延，还是无限广延或永恒存在的物质，或其中任何一者、或全部合起来，都不能是上帝。*199因为，

空间，与占有它、充塞它的事物分开来看，只是一幅空荡的布景或真空；说无限空间是上帝、或上帝是无限空间，就等于说祂是一个无限的真空——再没有比这更荒谬、更渎神的了。空间既只是一片浩瀚的虚空，与其说是任何实在的东西，不如说是一切事物的否定、一种弥散的虚无——它怎么能是第一因等等，乃至任何原因呢？除了可入性与广延，它还能有什么属性、什么卓越、什么完善呢？200

正如无限空间不能是上帝——尽管没有任何地方或空间把祂排除在外；同样，尽管祂是永恒的，永恒或无限的绵延本身也不是上帝。201因为绵延抽去一切持续之物，便不是什么实际自存的东西：它是一个存在者的绵延，不是一个存在者。

无限空间与绵延合在一起也不能是上帝：因为无边的空间加上无限的绵延，仍然只是永恒的空间，而至多不过一个永恒的真空。

===Original===

Since it has been already proved that corporeity is inconsistent with Divine perfection, though matter should be infinitely extended or there should be an infinite quantity of it, yet still, wherever it is, it carries this inconsistence along with it.

If to matter be added infinite duration, neither does this alter the nature of it. This only supposes it to be eternally what it is, i.e. eternally incapable of Divine perfection.

And if to it you add the ideas of both infinite extension (or space) and duration too, yet still, so long as matter is matter, it must always and everywhere be incapable of Divinity.

Lastly, not the universe, or sum total of finite beings, can be God. For if it is, then everything is divine, everything God, or of God; and so all things together must make but one being.202 But the contrary to this we see: there being evidently many beings distinct, and separable one from another, and independent each of other. Nay, this distinction and separation of existence, besides what we see without us, we may even feel within ourselves. We are severally conscious to ourselves of the individuation and distinction of our own minds from all other: nor is there anything of which we can be more certain. Were we all the same being, and had one mind, as in that case we must have, thoughts could not be private, or the peculiar thoughts of any one person, but they must be common acts of the whole mind, and there could be but one conscience common to us all.203 Besides, if all things conjunctly are God or the Perfect being (I dread the mention of such things, though it be in order to refute them), how comes this remarkable instance of imperfection, among many others, to cleave to us: that we should not know even ourselves, and what we are?204 In short, no collection of beings can be one being; and therefore not God. And the universe itself is but a collection of distinct beings.205

===Chinese===

既然已经证明形体性与神性的完善不相容，那么纵使物质无限广延、或其量无限，它无论在哪里，都把这不相容带在身上。

给物质再加上无限的绵延，也改变不了它的本性。这只是设想它永远是它之所是，即永远不能有神性的完善。

而若再给它加上无限广延（或空间）与绵延两个观念，那么只要物质还是物质，它就永远、处处不能有神性。

最后，宇宙、即有限存在者的总和，也不能是上帝。因为若是，则一切都是神圣的，一切都是上帝、或属上帝；于是万物合起来必只构成一个存在者。202但我们看到的却相反：显然有许多存在者，彼此有别、可相分离、各不相依。不，这种存在上的分别与隔离，除了身外所见，我们甚至在自己心中就能感到。我们各自意识到自己心灵的个体性与对其余一切的分别；没有比这更确定的事了。倘若我们都是同一个存在者、共有同一个心灵——那样我们就必得如此——思想便不能是私己的、不能是任何个人独有的思想，而必是整个心灵的共同行为，而且我们全体只能共有同一个良知。203此外，倘若万物合起来就是上帝或那完善者（我惮于提及此类说法，尽管是为了驳斥它们），那么，我们身上这许多不完善之中这显著的一例——我们竟连自己、连自己是什么都不知道204——又从何而来？简言之，任何存在者的集合都不能是一个存在者；因此不能是上帝。而宇宙本身不过是一群各别的存在者。205

===Original===

XIII. *It is so far from being true that God is corporeal, that there could be no such thing as either matter or motion, if there was not some Superior being upon whom they depended.* Or, *God is such a being, that without Him there could be neither matter nor motion.* This must be true of matter, because it has been proved already that there can be but one independent being, that he is incorporeal, and that the existence of all other beings must depend upon Him. But the same thing may be proved otherwise: If matter (I mean the existence of it) does not depend upon something above it, it must be an independent being; and if an independent being, a necessary being; and then there could be no such thing as a vacuum, but all bodies must be perfectly solid; and, more than that, the whole world could be but one such body, five times as firm as brass, and incapable of all motion. For that being which exists necessarily does necessarily exist: that is, it cannot *not* exist. But in a vacuum matter does not exist.

Moreover, if matter be an independent, necessary being, and exists of itself, this must be true of every particle of it; and if so, there could not only be no vacuum, but every particle must be everywhere. For it could not be limited to occupy only a place of such certain dimensions by its own nature, since this confinement of existence within certain bounds implies nonexistence in other places, beyond those bounds, and is equal to a negation of existence; and when existence is essential to any being, a negation of existence cannot be so. Nor, in the next place, could its existence be limited by anything else, because it is supposed to have its existence only of itself: i.e. to have a principle of existence in itself, or to have an existence that is not dependent upon or obnoxious to any other.

And, I may add still, if matter be self-existent, I do not see, not only how it comes to be restrained to a place of some certain capacity, but also how it comes to be limited in other respects, or why it should not exist in a manner that is in all respects perfect. So that thus it appears, matter must derive its existence from some other being, who causes it to be just what it is. And the being who can do this must be God.

===Chinese===

十三、*非但上帝不是有形的这一点为真，而且倘若没有一个使物质与运动所系于其上的更高存在者，就根本不会有物质或运动这回事。*或者说，*上帝是这样的存在者：没有祂，就既无物质也无运动。*就物质而言这必为真，因为已经证明只能有一个独立的存在者，祂无形体，而其余一切存在者的存在必系于祂。但这一点也可另证：倘若物质（我指其存在）不系于某个高于它的东西，它就必是一个独立的存在者；而若是独立的存在者，便是必然的存在者；那么就不可能有真空这回事，一切物体必是绝对坚实的；不仅如此，整个世界只能是这样的一个物体，比黄铜坚固五倍， incapable of all motion 一切运动皆无可能。因为必然存在者必然而存在：也就是说，它不能*不存在*。但在真空中物质并不存在。

再者，倘若物质是独立的、必然的存在者、凭自身而存在，那么它的每一粒都必如此；若是这样，则不仅没有真空，而且每一粒必处处存在。因为它不能凭自己的本性被限定于只占据某个确定维度的处所，因为把存在禁限于某些界限之内，就意味着在界限之外的别处不存在，等于对存在的否定；而当存在是某存在者的本质时，对存在的否定便不可能如此。其次，它的存在也不能被任何别物限定，因为它被设想为只凭自身而存在：即它自身之内有一个存在原理，或者说它的存在不依赖、也不受制于任何他者。

我还可以补充：倘若物质自有永有，我便不明白，它不仅何以被约束于某个有限容量的处所，而且在其他方面何以受限，何以不以一种在各方面都完善的方式存在。由此可见，物质必从某个别的存在者获得其存在，那存在者使它恰为其所是。而能做到这一点的存在者，必是上帝。

===Original===

It is to no purpose to object here that one cannot conceive how the existence of matter can be derived from another being. For God, being above our conceptions, the manner in which He operates, and in which things depend upon him, must also be inconceivable. Reason discovers that this visible world must owe its existence to some invisible Almighty being: i.e. it discovers this to be fact, and we must not deny facts because we know not *how* they are effected. It is far from being new, that our faculties should disclose to us the existence of things, and then drop us in our inquiry *how* they are. Thus much for matter.

As for *motion*: without a First cause, such as has been described, there could be none; and much less such motions as we see in the world. This may be immediately deduced from the foregoing paragraphs. For if matter itself could not be without such a cause, it is certain motion, which is an affection of matter, could never be.

But further, there could be no motion, unless either there be in matter itself a power of beginning it; or it is communicated from body to body in an infinite succession, or in a circle, and so has no beginning; or else is produced by some incorporeal being, or beings. Now as hardy as men are in advancing opinions that favor their vices, though never so repugnant to reason, I can hardly believe anyone will assert that a parcel of mere matter (let it be great or small, of any figure whatsoever, etc.) left altogether to itself, could ever of itself begin to move. If there is any such bold assertor, let him fix his eyes upon some lump of matter, e.g. a stone, piece of timber, or a clod (cleared of all animals), and peruse it well; and then, ask himself seriously whether it is possible for him in earnest to believe that that stone, log, or clod, though nothing corporeal or incorporeal should excite or meddle with it, might some time or other of itself begin to creep. However, to be short, a power of beginning motion is not in the idea of matter. It is passive, as we see, to the impressions of motion, and susceptive of it, but cannot produce it. On the contrary, it will always persist uniformly in its present state, either of rest or motion, if nothing stirs, diverts, accelerates, or stops it. Nor is there anything in all physics better settled than that which is called *vis inertiae* or the inertia of matter.

===Chinese===

在此反驳说「不能设想物质的存在如何从另一个存在者得来」，是无济于事的。因为上帝既高于我们的领会，祂运作的方式、事物系于祂的方式，也必不可设想。理性发现这个可见的世界必把它的存在归功于某个不可见的全能者：也就是说，理性发现这是事实，而我们不可因为不知其*如何*实现便否认事实。我们的官能向我们揭示事物的存在、然后在我们追问其*如何*时弃我们而去，这绝非新鲜事。关于物质就说这么多。

至于*运动*：没有前面描述的那样的第一因，就不可能有运动；更不会有我们在世上所见的那些运动。这可以从前几段直接推出。因为倘若连物质本身都离不了这样一个原因，那么运动——它只是物质的一种情态——就更不可能有。

但更进一步说，若无下列情况之一，便不能有运动：或物质自身之中有发起运动的能力；或运动在物体之间无限相继地、或在一个圆圈中传递，从而没有开端；或运动由某个无形体的存在者或存在者们产生。人们虽勇于提出种种有利于其恶欲的见解、哪怕与理性如何相悖，我仍难相信有谁会断言：一团纯粹的物质（无论大小、无论什么形状等等）完全被撇下不管，竟能凭自己开始运动。倘真有这样大胆的断言者，就让他盯着某一团物质，比如一块石头、一段木头或一块土疙瘩（清除其中一切动物）细看一番；然后郑重地问自己：他可真能相信那块石头、木头或土疙瘩，纵然没有任何有形或无形之物搅动它、招惹它，有朝一日竟会自己开始爬动。然而长话短说：发起运动的能力并不在物质的观念之中。物质正如我们所见，对运动的印象是被动的、可承受的，但不能产生运动。相反，若无东西拨动它、使它转向、加速或停止，它将始终一致地保持其现有的静止或运动状态。而物理学中再没有比所谓*vis inertiae*、即物质的惰性更确定不移的了。

===Original===

The propagation of motion from body to body, without any First mover, or immaterial cause of motion, has been proved impossible, proposition I.

The supposition of a perpetual motion in a circle is begging the question. For if A moves B, B moves C, and so on to Z, and then Z moves A; this is the same as to say that A moves A, by the intervention of B, C, D,﻿ ﻿… Z: that is, A moves itself, or can begin motion.206

It remains then, that all corporeal motions come originally from some mover incorporeal, which must be either that Supreme and self-existing spirit himself, who is God, or such as will put us into the way how to find that there is such a Being (turn back to proposition I).

If we consider ourselves, and the voluntary motions begun by us, we may there see the thing exemplified. We move our bodies, or some members of them, and by these move other things, as they again do others, and know these motions to spring from the operations of our minds; but then we know also, that we have not an independent power of creating motion. If we had, it could not be so limited as our locomotive faculties are, nor confined to small quantities and certain circumstances only: we should have had it from eternity, nor could we ever be deprived of it. So that we are necessitated to look up and acknowledge some Higher being, who is able not only to produce motion, but to impart a faculty of producing it.

And if the petty motions of us mortals afford arguments for the being of a God, much more may those greater motions we see in the world, and the phenomena attending them: I mean the motions of the planets and heavenly bodies. For these must be put into motion, either by one common mighty Mover, acting upon them immediately, or by causes and laws of His appointment, or by their respective movers, who, for reasons to which you can by this time be no stranger, must depend upon some Superior, that furnish them with the power of doing this. And granting it to be done either of these ways, we can be at no great distance from a demonstration of the existence of a Deity.

===Chinese===

运动若无最初推动者、无非物质的运动原因而只在物体间传递，已被命题一证明为不可能。

设想一种永恒的圆圈式运动，乃是乞题。因为若 A 推动 B，B 推动 C，如此至 Z，然后 Z 又推动 A；这就等于说 A 借 B、C、D、…、Z 之中介推动 A：也就是说，A 推动它自己，或能发起运动。206

于是只剩：一切形体运动原本都出自某个非物质的推动者——祂或是那自有永有的至高灵本身、即上帝，或是那种能把我们引向发现有这样一位存在者的推动者（回看命题一）。

我们若反观自己、反观由我们发起的随意运动，便可看见实例。我们移动自己的身体或某些肢体，又借它们移动他物，它们再移动物物，并知道这些运动源自我们心灵的活动；但我们也知道，我们并没有一种独立创造运动的能力。倘若有，它就不会像我们的运动官能这样受限、不会只限于小量和某些情形：我们必从永恒就拥有它，也永远不会失去它。所以我们不能不仰望并承认某个更高的存在者，祂不仅能产生运动，还能授予产生运动的官能。

倘若我们这些凡人的微小运动已足为上帝之存在提供论证，那么我们在世上所见更大的运动、及其相伴的现象——我指行星与天体的运动——就更加如此。因为这些天体必被推动：或由一位共同的伟大推动者直接作用于它们，或由祂所定的原因与法则，或由各自的推动者——而出于你们此时已不陌生的理由，这些推动者必系于某个更高者，由祂赋予他们这样做的能力。而无论承认是其中哪一种方式，我们离神性存在的证明都已不远。

===Original===

It may perhaps be said that though matter has not the power of moving itself, yet it has an attractive force by which it can move other parts of matter, so that all matter equally moves and is moved. But, allowing those things which are now usually ascribed to attraction, we shall still be necessitated to own some Superior being whose influence mixes itself with matter, and operates upon it, or at least who, some way or other, imparts this force. For attraction, according to the true sense of the word, supposes one body to act upon another at a distance, or where it is not; but nothing can be an agent, where it is not at all. Matter can act only by contact, impelling contiguous bodies, when it is put into motion by something else, or resisting those which strike against it, when it is at rest. And this it does as matter: i.e. by being impenetrable to other matter; but attraction is not of the nature or idea of matter. So that what is called “attraction,” is so called only because the same things happen as if the parts of matter did mutually attract; but in truth this can only be an effect of something which acts upon or by matter according to a certain law. The parts of matter seem not only to gravitate towards each other, but many of them to fly each other. Now these two contrary motions and seeming qualities cannot both proceed from matter *quà* matter; cannot both be of the nature of it: and therefore they must be owing to some external cause, or to some other being, which excites in them this as it were love and discord.207

Besides, as to the revolution of a planet about the sun, mere gravitation is not sufficient to produce that effect. It must be compounded with a motion of projection, to keep the planet from falling directly into the sun, and bring it about; and from what hand, I desire to know, comes this other motion (or direction)? Who impressed it?

What a vast field for contemplation is here opened! Such regions of matter about us, in which there is not the least particle that does not carry with it an argument of God’s existence; not the least stick or straw, or other trifle that falls to the ground, but shows it; not the slightest motion produced, the least whisper of the air, but tells it.

===Chinese===

或许有人会说：物质虽然没有推动自己的能力，却有一种吸引之力，能推动物质的其他部分，所以一切物质既推动又被推动。但是，即便承认如今通常归于吸引的那些现象，我们仍不得不承认某个更高的存在者，祂的影响渗入物质、作用于物质，或者至少以某种方式授予这种力量。因为照「吸引」一词的真义，它设想一个物体在远处、在它不在的地方作用于另一个物体；但没有任何东西能在它根本不在的地方作动因。物质只能凭接触行动：被别物推入运动时冲撞相邻的物体，或静止时抵抗撞向它的物体。而这是物质*作为物质*做到的：即凭借对其他物质的不可入性；吸引却不属于物质的本性或观念。所以，所谓「吸引」之所以如此称呼，只是因为发生的事情仿佛物质的各部分在相互吸引；而实际上这只能是某个依某种法则作用于物质、或借物质运作的东西的效果。物质的各部分似乎不仅彼此相坠，其中许多还彼此相避。这两种相反的运动与貌似相反的性质，不可能都出自物质*qua*（作为）物质；不可能都是物质的本性：因此它们必归于某个外在的原因、某个别的存在者，是它在它们之中激起这仿佛爱与不和的东西。207

此外，就行星绕太阳的运转而言，单凭坠向不足以产生那个效果。它必须与一个横向投射的运动复合，才能使行星不致径直坠入太阳，而绕之运转；我倒要问问，这另一个运动（或方向）来自何方之手？是谁赋予的？

这里展开了一片何等浩瀚的沉思之野！我们四周有这样广阔的物质之域，其中没有一粒微尘不随身携带着上帝存在的论证；没有一根最细的棍子或草、或任何落向地面的小东西不显示它；没有一次最轻微的运动、一缕最轻微的空气低语不在诉说它。

===Original===

XIV. *The frame and constitution of the world, the magnificence of it, the various phenomena and kinds of beings, the uniformity observed in the productions of things, the uses and ends for which they serve, etc., do all show that there is some Almighty designer, an infinite wisdom and power at the top of all these things: such marks there are of both.*208 or, *God is that Being, without whom such a frame or constitution of the world, such a magnificence in it, etc., could not be.

===Chinese===

十四、*世界的架构与构造、它的壮丽、种种现象与存在者的类别、事物产生中所见的齐一性、它们所服务的用途与目的等等，都表明有一位全能的设计者、一种无限的智慧与能力高踞于这一切之上：二者都有这样的印记。*208或者说，*上帝是这样的存在者：没有祂，这样的世界架构或构造、这样的壮丽等等，便不可能有。

===Original===

* In order to prove to anyone the grandness of this fabric of the world, one needs only to bid him consider the sun, with that insupportable glory and lustre that surrounds it; to demonstrate the vast distance, magnitude, and heat of it; to represent to him the chorus of planets moving periodically, by uniform laws, in their several orbits about it, affording a regular variety of aspects, guarded some of them by secondary planets, and, as it were, emulating the state of the sun, and probably all possessed by proper inhabitants; to remind him of those surprising visits the comets make us, the large trains, or uncommon splendor, which attends them, the far country they come from, and the curiosity and horror they excite not only among us, but in the inhabitants of other planets, who also may be up to see the entry and progress of these ministers of fate;209 to direct his eye and contemplation through those azure fields and vast regions above him, up to the fixed stars, that radiant numberless host of heaven, and to make him understand how unlikely a thing it is that they should be placed there only to adorn and bespangle a canopy over our heads (though that would be a great piece of magnificence too), and much less to supply the places of so many glowworms, by affording a feeble light to our earth, or even to all our fellow-planets; to convince him, that they are rather so many other suns, with their several regions and sets of planets about them; to show him, by the help of glasses, still more and more of these fixed lights, and to beget in him an apprehension of their unaccountable numbers, and of those immense spaces that lie retired beyond our utmost reach and even imagination﻿—I say, one needs but to do this, and explain to him such things as are now known almost to everybody, and by it to show that if the world be not infinite, it is *infinito similis*,210 and therefore sure a magnificent structure, and the work of an infinite Architect. But if we could take a view of all the particulars contained within that astonishing compass, which we have thus hastily run over, how would wonders multiply upon us? Every corner, every part of the world is as it were made up of other worlds. If we look upon this, our seat (I mean this earth), what scope is here for admiration? The great variety of mountains, hills, valleys, plains, rivers, seas, trees, plants!

===Chinese===

要向人证明这个世界构造之宏伟，只须请他想想太阳，及其周围那不可逼视的光辉与灿亮；向他论证太阳那浩渺的距离、巨大的体积与炽热；为他描绘行星的行列按齐一的法则周期性地在各自的轨道上绕日运行，呈现出规则的种种相位，其中一些还有次级行星护卫，仿佛 emulate 太阳的尊仪，而且很可能都栖有相宜的居民；提醒他彗星对我们作的那些惊人造访、随行的长大彗尾或异常光彩、它们所自来的遥远乡域、以及它们不仅在我们要在别的行星居民中激起的好奇与惊骇——那些居民或许也正仰望这些命运使者209的入场与行进；引导他的目光与沉思穿过头顶那些蔚蓝的原野与广袤的天域，上达恒星——天空中那光辉灿烂、不可胜数的大军——并使他明白：把它们安置在那里仅仅为了装点我们头顶的华盖（尽管那也已是了不起的壮丽）、更不必说仅仅为了充当那么多萤火虫、给我们的地球乃至一切同行行星提供微弱的光，是多么不可能的事；让他确信，它们册宁是那么多别的太阳，各有自己的天域与成群的行星绕行；借望远镜向他显示愈来愈多的这些恒星之光，使他对它们那无从索解的数目、以及对那些深藏于我们极力所及乃至想象之外的浩瀚空间，生出一种领会——我说，人只须做到这些，向他讲解如今几乎人人皆知的事情，并由此表明：这个世界即使不是无限的，也是*infinito similis*（类似无限）210的东西，因而确是一件宏伟的结构、出自一位无限的建筑师之手。而倘若我们能细看这仓促掠过的惊人范围内的一切细节，惊奇又会在我们身上怎样成倍地涌出？世界的每一个角落、每一部分都仿佛由别的世界组成。倘若我们观看我们的这个居所（我指这地球），这里有多少可供惊叹的余地！山川、丘陵、溪谷、平原、江河、海洋、草木，何其多样！

===Original===

The many tribes of different animals with which it is flocked! The multifarious inventions and works of one of these; that is, of us men, etc. And yet when all these (heaven and earth) are surveyed as nicely as they can be by the help of our unassisted senses, and even of telescopical glasses, by the assistance of good microscopes in very small parts of matter as many new wonders211 may perhaps be discovered, as those already observed: new kingdoms of animals, new architecture and curiosity of work. So that, as before our senses and even conception fainted in those vast journeys we were obliged to take in considering the expanse of the universe, so here again they fail us in our researches into the principles and consistuent parts of it. Both the beginnings and the ends of things, the least and the greatest, all conspire to baffle us, and, which way ever we prosecute our inquiries, we still fall in with fresh subjects of amazement, and fresh reasons to believe that there are indefinitely still more, and more behind, that will forever escape our eagerest pursuits and deepest penetration.

===Chinese===

栖息其上的动物各族何其繁伙！其中一族——就是我们人类——的发明与作品又何其繁多！而当这一切（天与地）已被我们仅凭肉眼，甚至借望远镜尽可能地考察之后，再借助良好的显微镜观察物质至微之处，还可能发现同已观察到的同样多的新惊奇211：新的动物王国，新的构造之巧妙与工艺之精奇。于是，正如在我们不得不作的那些遨游宇宙广袤的旅行中、我们的感官乃至概念都晕眩了一样，在这里，当我们探究它的原理与组成成分时，它们又一次不管用了。事物之始与末、最小者与最大者，都合力难倒我们；而无论我们朝哪个方向推进探究，总不断遇到新的可惊之物、新的理由，使我们相信在这一切之后还有无限更多、永远逃出我们最热切的追求与最深刻的洞穿之力的东西。

===Original===

This mighty building is not only thus grand, and the appearances stupendous in it, but the *manner* in which things are effected is commonly unintelligible, and their causes too profound for us. There are indeed many things in nature which we know, and some of which we seem to know the causes, but, alas! how few are these with respect to the whole sum? And the causes which we assign, what are they? Commonly such, as can only be expressed in general terms, while the bottoms of things remain unfathomable. Such as have been collected from experience, but could scarcely be known beforehand, by any arguments *a priori*, to be capable of rendering such effects; and yet till causes are known after that manner, they are not thoroughly understood. Such, as seem disproportionate and too little, and are so insufficient and unsatisfactory, that one cannot but be inclined to think that something immaterial and invisible must be immediately concerned. In short, we know many times that such a thing will have such an effect, or perhaps that such an effect is produced by such a cause, but the manner *how* we know not, or but grossly, and if such an hypothesis be true. It is impossible for us to come at the true principles of things, or to see into the economy of the finest part of nature and workings of the first springs. The causes that appear to us, are but effects of other causes; the vessels of which the bodies of plants and animals consist, are made up of other, smaller vessels; the subtlest parts of matter which we have any notion of (as animal spirits, or particles of light), have *their* parts, and may for ought we know be compound bodies; and, as to the substances themselves of all these things, and their internal constitution, they are hid from our eyes. Our philosophy dwells in the surface of nature.

However, in the next place, we ourselves cannot but be witnesses that there are stated methods, as so many set forms of proceeding, which things punctually and religiously keep to. The same causes, circumstanced in the same manner, have always the same success; all the species of animals among us, are made according to one general idea; and so are those of plants also, and even minerals: no new ones are brought forth or arisen anywhere, and the old are preserved and continued by the old ways.

===Chinese===

这座巨厦不仅如此宏伟、其中的景象如此惊人，而且事物得以成就的*方式*通常不可索解，其原因也深不可测。自然中诚然有许多我们知道的东西，有一些我们还似乎知道其原因，可是，唉！比起全部总和，这些又是何其少？而我们指出的那些原因又是什么？通常只是些只能以笼统言辞表述的东西，而事物的底蕴依然无由穷究。有些原因得自经验，却很难凭任何*先验的*论证预知其能产生这样的结果；而原因非到那样被认识，就不算被彻底理解。有些原因显得不相称而太小，如此不充分、不令人满意，以致人不能不倾向于认为，必有某种非物质、不可见的东西直接参与其间。简言之，我们常常知道某物将有某效果，或某效果由某原因产生，但那*如何*产生的方式，我们不知道，或只粗略地知道，而且还是假如那个假说为真的话。我们不可能触及事物的真正原理，不可能看透自然最精微部分的结构与最初发条的运作。我们所见的原因，只是别的原因的结果；构成动植物身体的那些管道，又由别的更细的管道组成；我们对之稍有观念的最精微的物质部分（如动物精气、光的微粒），也各有其部分，而且就我们所知也可能是复合体；至于这一切事物的实体本身及其内部构造，则对我们隐藏不见。我们的哲学栖居在自然的表面。

然而，其次，我们自己不能不作证：存在着既定的方法，仿佛种种规定的行事程式，事物一板一眼、一丝不苟地遵循着。同样的原因、在同样的情形之下，总有同样的结果；我们中间一切动物的物种，都按同一个一般的观念造成；植物如此，矿物亦然：任何地方都不曾产生或出现新的物种，旧的物种又都循旧路得以保存与延续。

===Original===

Lastly, it appears, I think plainly enough, in the parts and model of the world, that there is a *contrivance* and a respect to certain reasons and *ends*. How the sun is posited near the middle of our system for the more convenient dispensing of his benign influences to the planets moving about him; how the plain of the earth’s equator intersects that of her orbit, and makes a proper angle with it, in order to diversify the year and create a useful variety of seasons, and many other things of this kind, though a thousand times repeated, will always be pleasing meditations to good men and true scholars. Who can observe the vapors to ascend, especially from the sea, meet above in clouds, and fall again after condensation, and not understand this to be a kind of distillation in order to clear the water of its grosser salts, and then by rains and dews to supply the fountains and rivers with fresh and wholesome liquor, to nourish the vegetables below by showers which descend in drops as from a watering-pot upon a garden, etc.; who can view the structure of a plant or animal, the indefinite number of their fibers and fine vessels, the formation of larger vessels and the several members out of them, and the apt disposition of all these, the way laid out for the reception and distribution of nutriment, the effect this nutriment has in extending the vessels, bringing the vegetable or animal to its full growth and expansion, continuing the motion of the several fluids, repairing the decays of the body, and preserving life; who can take notice of the several faculties of animals, their arts of saving and providing for themselves, or the ways in which they are provided for, the uses of plants to animals, and of some animals to others, particularly to mankind, the care taken that the several species should be propagated out of their proper seeds (without confusion),212 the strong inclinations implanted in animals for that purpose, their love of their young, and the like; I say, who can do this, and not see a *design*, in such regular pieces, so nicely wrought, and so preserved?

===Chinese===

最后，我认为足够显然：在世界的各个部分与整体设计之中，有一种*匠心*、一种对某些理由与*目的*的顾念。太阳如何被安置在我们体系的近中心处，以便更便利地把它的惠泽播撒给绕之运行的诸行星；地球赤道平面如何与轨道平面相交、与之成一个合适的角度，以使年岁有别、造出有用的季节更替，以及诸如此类的许多事，虽经千遍重复，将永远是善人与真学者的惬意沉思。谁能观察水汽——尤其自海面——上升，在高空会聚为云，冷凝之后复又落下，而不明白这是一种蒸馏，为的是把水中较粗的盐分澄清，然后借雨水与露水以新鲜卫生的水补给泉源与江河，像浇花园的水壶那样滴落的阵雨滋养下方的草木，等等；谁能观看一株植物或一只动物的构造、它们无数的纤维与精微的管道、较大的管道与各个器官如何由之而成、这一切的巧妙配置、为接受与输送养分而铺设的道路、这养分在扩展管道、把植物或动物带到完全的长成与舒展、维持各种体液的运行、修补身体的耗损、保存生命方面的功效；谁能留意动物的各种官能、它们自存自备的技巧、或它们受供应的方式、植物之于动物、某些动物之于其他动物——尤其是之于人类——的用途、对诸物种各从其类（不相混杂）212由种子传衍212所下的功夫、为此植入动物体内的强烈冲动、它们对幼崽的爱恋等等——我说，谁能做到这些，而看不见在这样规整、这样精巧、又这样被保全的作品中的*设计*呢？

===Original===

If there was but *one* animal, and in that case it could not be doubted but that his eyes were made that he might see with them, his ears that he might hear with them, and so on, through at least the most considerable parts of him; if it can much less be doubted, when the same things are repeated in the individuals of all the tribes of animals; if the like observations may be made with respect to vegetables, and other things; and if all these kinds of things, and therefore much more their particulars, upon and in the earth, waters, air, are inconceivably numerous (as most evidently they are), one cannot but be convinced from that, which is so very obvious to every understanding, and plainly runs through the nobler parts of the visible world, that not only they, but other things, even those that seem to be less noble, have their ends too, though not so well understood.

And now, since we cannot suppose the parts of matter to have contrived this wonderful form of a world among themselves, and then by agreement to have taken their respective posts, and pursued constant ends by certain methods and measures concerted (because these are acts of which they are not capable), there must be some other Being, whose wisdom and power are equal to such a mighty work as is the structure and preservation of the world. There must be some almighty Mind, who models and adorns it, lays the causes of things so deep, prescribes them such uniform and steady laws, destines and adapts them to certain purposes, and makes one thing to fit and answer to another.213

===Chinese===

倘若世上*只有一只*动物，那么它的眼睛是为了使它看得见、耳朵是为了使它听得见等等，至少就其最重要的部分而言，就不容怀疑；当同样的事在动物各族的个体中反复出现时，就更少可疑；倘若对植物和其他事物也可作同样的观察；而这一切东西——因而更其它们的个体——遍布于地上、水中、空气，其数目不可胜计（这最为显然），那么，人就不能不被说服：这桩对每个理智都如此显明、显然贯穿于可见世界之较高贵部分的事，不仅它们有目的，其他事物、连那些看似较不高贵的，也有其目的，只是不为我们所深知。

而既然我们不能设想物质的部分能自行谋划出世界这一奇妙的形式、然后经约定各就其位、依商定的方法与尺度追求恒常的目的（因为这些是它们办不到的事），就必存在另外某位存在者，其智慧与能力足以承担世界之构造与保存这样伟大的工程。必有一颗全能的心智，为世界造型并加修饰，把事物的原因安置得这样深，为它们规定这样齐一而稳定的法则，命定它们达于某些目的，使一物与另一物相称相合。213

===Original===

That such a beautiful scheme, such a just and geometrical arrangement of things, composed of innumerable parts, and placed as the offices and uses and wants of the several beings require, through such an immense extent, should be the effect of *chance* only, is a conceit so prodigiously absurd that certainly no one can espouse it heartily, who understands the meaning of that word. “Chance” seems to be only a term by which we express our ignorance of the cause of anything. For when we say anything comes “by chance,” we do not mean that it had no other cause, but only that we do not know the true cause which produced it, or interposed in such a manner as to make that fall out which was not expected. Nor can I think that anybody has such an idea of chance, as to make it an *agent* or really existing and acting cause of anything, and much less sure of *all* things. Whatever events or effects there are, they must proceed from some agent or cause, which is either free or not free (that is, necessary). If it be free, it wills what it produces, and therefore that which is produced is produced with design, not by chance. If it acts necessarily, the event must necessarily be, and therefore it is not by accident. For that which is by accident or chance only, might not have been; or, it is an accident only that it is. There can be therefore no such cause as chance. And to omit a great deal that might yet be said, matter is indefinitely divisible, and the first particles (or atoms) of which it consists must be small beyond all our apprehension; and the chances that must all hit to produce *one* individual of any species of material beings (if only chance was concerned), must consequently be indefinitely many; and if space be also indefinitely extended, and the number of those individuals (not to say of the species themselves) which lie dispersed in it indefinite, the chances required to the production of them all, or of the universe, will be the rectangle of one indefinite quantity drawn into another. We may well call them infinite. And then, to say that anything cannot happen unless infinite chances coincide, is the same as to say there are infinite chances against the happening of it, or odds that it will not happen; and this, again, is the same as to say it is impossible to happen, since if there be a possibility that it may happen, the hazard is not infinite.

===Chinese===

说这样一个美妙的方案、这样一个由无数部分组成、安置得恰合各存在者的职分、用途与需要、绵亘于如此浩瀚范围之内的精确而合乎几何的安排，竟然只是*偶然*的产物——这种想法荒谬绝伦，凡懂得「偶然」一词含义的人，决不会真心拥抱它。「偶然」似乎只是一个词，我们借以表达自己对某事物原因的无知。因为当我们说某事「出于偶然」，我们并不是说它没有别的原因，而只是说我们不知道产生它的真正原因，或不知道有某物如此介入、使那未可预料的事落了出来。我也不认为谁会有这样的「偶然」观念，把它当作一个*能动者*、一个实际存在而起作用的原因——更不必说*万物*的原因了。凡有事件或结果，必出自某个能动者或原因，它或是自由的、或是不自由的（即必然的）。若是自由的，它意愿它所产生的，因而所产生者是带着设计产生的，而非出于偶然。若它必然地起作用，结果就必然而然，因而并非出于偶然。因为凡仅出于偶然的事，都可能不曾发生；或者说，它的发生只是偶然。所以不可能有「偶然」这样的原因。且撇下还可说的许多话不谈：物质可无限分割，组成物质的第一微粒（原子）必小得超出我们的一切领会；而（倘若只有偶然参与）要产生任一物质物种的*一个*个体所必须全部命中的机会，必因而是无限多的；倘若空间又无限广延、散布其中的那些个体（更不必说物种本身）之数无限，则产生它们全体、即产生宇宙所需的机会，将是一个不确定量乘另一个不确定量的乘积。我们尽可以称之为无限。而说一件事非有无限的机会相合便不能发生，就等于说有无限的机会反对它发生、或者说它不发生的胜算无限；而这又等于说它不可能发生——因为倘若它有发生的可能，风险便不是无限的。

===Original===

The world therefore cannot be the child of chance.214 He must be little acquainted with the works of nature, who is not sensible how delicate and fine they are; and the finer they are, the grosser were those of Epicurus.215

If it should be objected that many things seem to be useless, many births are monstrous, or the like, such answers as these may be made: The uses of some things are known to some men, and not to others; the uses of some are known now, that were not known to anybody formerly; the uses of many may be discovered hereafter; and those of some other things may forever remain unknown to all men, and yet be in nature, as much as those discovered were before their discovery, or are now in respect of them who know them not. Things have not, therefore, no uses, because they are concealed from us. Nor is nature irregular, or without method, because there are some seeming deviations from the common rule. These are generally the effects of that influence which free agents and various circumstances have upon natural productions, which may be deformed or hurt by external impressions, heterogeneous matter introduced, or disagreeable and unnatural motions excited; and if the case could be truly put, it would no doubt appear that nature proceeds as regularly (or the laws of nature have as regular an effect), when a monster is produced, as when the usual issue in common cases. Under these circumstances the monster is the *genuine* issue: that is, in the same circumstances there would always be the same kind of production. And, therefore, if things are now and then misshaped, this infers no unsteadiness or mistake in nature. Besides, the magnificence of the world admits of some *perturbations*; not to say, requires some *variety*. The question is: Could all those things, which we *do know* to have uses and ends, and to the production of which such wonderful contrivance and the combinations of so many things are required, be produced, and method and regularity be preserved *so far as it is*, if nothing but blind chance presided over all? Are not the innumerable instances of things which are undeniably made with reference to certain ends, and of those which are propagated and repeated by the same constant methods, enough to convince us that there are ends proposed, and rules observed, even where we do not see them?

===Chinese===

因此，世界不可能是偶然之子。214凡对自然的作品不感到其精妙细微者，必是对它们所知甚少；而作品愈精妙，伊壁鸠鲁215的作品便愈粗陋。

若有人反驳说：许多东西似乎无用，许多产育怪异，等等；可以这样回答：有些东西的用途，为此人所知而为彼人所不知；有些东西的用途现在为人所知，从前却无人知晓；许多东西的用途日后或可发现；还有些东西的用途也许永远无人知晓，却依然存在于自然之中——正如已发现的那些在发现之前、或在不知者看来也只是如此。所以，事物并不因被向我们隐藏了用途，就没有用途。自然也不因有某些貌似偏离常规之处，就不规则、就没有方法。这些偏离一般是自由能动者与种种情势对自然产物的影响所致，产物可能因外部印象、混入的异质物质、或激起的不合自然之运动而受损变形；而倘若案情能被如实陈述，无疑便会显出：产生怪胎时自然的运行同寻常情形下一样规则（或者说自然法则的效果一样规则）。在那些情形之下，怪胎乃是*真正的*产出：也就是说，同样的情形之下总会有同样种类的东西产生。因此，事物偶有畸变，并不意味着自然有什么不稳或差失。况且，世界的壮丽容得下一些*扰动*；甚至毋宁说需要一些*变化*。问题在于：那些我们*确实知道*有用途与目的、其产生需要那样奇妙的匠心与如此众多事物之组合的东西，倘若只有盲目的偶然主宰一切，还能够被产生出来、而且方法与规则还被保持到*如今这个地步*吗？那无数显然针对某些目的而造的事物、那无数以同一恒常方法传衍重复的事物，还不足以使我们确信——即便在我们看不见的地方，也有既定的目的、被遵守的规则吗？

And, lastly, if we should descend to particulars, what are those seemingly useless or monstrous productions in respect of the rest, that plainly declare the ends for which they were intended, and that come into the world by the usual ways, with the usual perfection of their several kinds? If the comparison could be made, I verily believe these would be found to be almost infinituple of the other, which ought therefore to be reputed as nothing.

They, who content themselves with words, may ascribe the formation of the world to “fate” or “nature,” as well as to chance, or better. And yet fate, in the first place, is nothing but a series of events, considered as necessarily following in some certain order, or of which it has always been true that they *would be* in their determinate times and places. It is called indeed a series of causes,216 but then they are such causes as are also effects﻿—all of them, if there is no First cause﻿—and may be taken for such. So that in this description is nothing like such a cause as is capable of giving this form to the world. A series of events is the same with events happening *seriatim*: which words declare nothing concerning the *cause* of that concatenation of events, or why it is. Time, place, manner, necessity are but *circumstances* of things that come to pass, not causes of their existence, or of their being as they are. On the contrary, some external and superior cause must be supposed to put the series in motion, to project the order, to connect the causes and effects, and to *impose* the necessity.217

Then for “nature,”

-

If it be used for the intrinsic manner of existing﻿—that constitution, make, or disposition, with which anything is produced or born, and from which result those properties, powers, inclinations, passions, qualities, and manners, which are called natural (and sometimes “nature”), in opposition to such as are acquired, adventitious, or forced (which use is common)﻿—then to say that nature formed anything, or gave it its manner of existence, is to say that it formed itself, or that the effect is the efficient.218 Besides, how can *manner* (manner of existing) be the cause of existing, or properly do anything. An agent is an acting being, some substance, not a *manner* of being.

最后，倘若我们下到细节：那些貌似无用或怪异的产物，比起其余那些明白宣告其受造之目的、且循常途而来、带着各自种类通常之完善的东西，又算得了什么？倘若能够比较，我深信后者几乎是前者的无穷倍，前者因此应视为无物。

满足于字眼的人，尽可以把世界的形成归于「命运」或「自然」，同归于偶然一样，甚至更好。然而命运，首先，无非是一串事件，被看作按某种确定的秩序必然相随，或其「将于其确定之时其确定之地*发生*」从来为真。它诚然被称为一串原因，216但那些原因同时也是结果——若没有第一因，则全是如此——而且也只能如此看待。所以这描述中丝毫没有那样一种原因的影子，能赋予世界这个形式。一串事件与事件*依次*发生是一回事：这些字眼对那事件连环的*原因*、或它何以如此，毫无所说。时间、地点、方式、必然性，只是发生之事的*情形*，不是它们存在、或它们如其所示的原因。相反，必须设想某个外在而更高的原因，把序列发动起来、设计出秩序、把原因与结果连结起来，并*赋予*那必然性。217

至于「自然」，

-

倘若它被用来指存在的内在方式——即某物产生或出生时所禀受的那个构造、体制或禀性，由之生出那些被称为自然的（有时也称作「本性」）属性、能力、倾向、激情、品质与习性，以别于那些获得的、偶发的或强加的（这种用法很常见）——那么说自然形成了某物、或给了它存在的方式，就是说它形成了它自己，或者说结果就是动因。218况且，*方式*（存在的方式）怎么能是存在的原因、或严格地做成任何事呢？能动者是一个行动着的存在者、某个实体，而不是存在的*方式*。

-

===Original===

If it be used in that other sense, by which it stands for the *ideas* of things, what they are in themselves, and what in their circumstances, causes, consequences, respects; or, in short, that which determines them to be of this or that kind (as when we say, the *nature* of justice219 requires this or that, i.e. the idea of justice requires or supposes it; a crime is of such a *nature*, that is, bears such a respect to the law, and is attended with such circumstances; or the like): then none of these senses can do an atheist any service.

-

If it be used for the *world*220 (as, the laws of *nature* may be understood to be the laws of the world, by which it is governed, and the phenomena in it produced; after the same manner of speaking as when we say, the laws of England, France, etc.) then it stands for that very thing, the former and architect of which is the object of our inquiry, and therefore cannot be that architect itself. Under this sense may be comprehended that, when it denotes *reality of existence*, as when it is said that such a thing is not in *nature* (not to be found in the world).

-

If it signifies the forementioned laws themselves, or that course in which things by virtue of these laws proceed (as when the effects of these laws are styled the works of *nature*), then, laws suppose some legislator, and are posterior to that of which they are the laws. There can be no laws of any nation, till the people are of which that nation consists.

-

If it be used after the same manner as the word “habit” frequently is, to which many things are ascribed (just as they are to nature), though it be nothing existing distinct from the habits which particular men or beings contract, then nature is a kind of abstract notion, which can *do* nothing. Perhaps “nature” may be put for *natures*, all natures, after the manner of a collective noun; or it may be mentioned as an *agent* only as we personify virtues and attributes, either for variety, or the shorter and more convenient expressing of things.

-

Lastly, if it denotes the Author of nature, or God221 (the effect seeming, though by a hard metonymy in this case, to be put for the efficient), then, to Him it is that I ascribe the formation of the world, etc.

===Chinese===

倘若它取另一种含义，指事物的*观念*——它们自身是什么、在其情形、原因、结果、关系中又是什么；或者简言之，那使它们成为这一类或那一类的东西（如我们说，正义之*本性*219要求这个或那个，即正义的观念要求或预设了它；某罪具有这样的*性质*，即它与法律有这样的关系、伴有这样的情形；等等）——那么这些含义没有一个能替无神论者效力。

-

倘若它指*世界*220（如自然之*法则*可理解为世界之法则、即支配世界并产生其中现象的法则；一如我们说英格兰的法则、法兰西的法则等等）——那么它所指的恰恰是那样一个东西，其创造者与建筑师正是我们探究的对象，因此它自己不能就是那位建筑师。此种含义之下也可包括：当它指*存在的实在*时，如说某物不在*自然之中*（在世上找不到）。

-

倘若它意指上述那些法则本身、或事物凭这些法则而行的进程（如这些法则的效果被称为*自然*的作品），那么，法则预设某位立法者，且后于其为法则所系的那个东西。一国之法，必待组成该国的人民存在之后才有。

-

倘若它的用法同「习惯」一词的常见用法一样——许多事情被归之于习惯（正如被归之于自然一样），尽管它并非独立于各人或各个存在者所养成的诸习惯之外的什么实存——那么自然就是一种抽象观念，它不能*做*任何事。或者「自然」也许代表*诸本性*、一切本性，作集合名词用；或者它被当作一个*能动者*被提到，只是像我们把德性与属性拟人化那样，或为行文变化、或为更简捷便利地表达事物。

-

最后，倘若它指自然之主宰、即上帝221（此情形中效果似乎是——尽管是种勉强的换喻——被用来指动因），那么，世界的形成等等，正是我归之于祂的。

To all which I must subjoin that there is an unaccountable liberty taken in the use of this word, and that frequently it is used merely as a word, and nothing more, they who use it not knowing themselves what they mean by it.222 However, in no sense can it supersede the being of a Deity.

XV. *Life, sense, agitation, and the faculties of our own minds show the existence of some superior Being from whom they are derived*, Or, *God is that Being, without whom neither could these be, any more than the things before mentioned*. That they cannot flow from the nature of any matter about us, as matter, or from any modification, size, or motion of it, if it be not already apparent, may perhaps be proved more fully afterwards. And that our souls themselves are not self-existent, nor hold their faculties independently of all other beings, follows from propositions IV and VII. Therefore, we must necessarily be indebted for what we have, of this kind, to some great Benefactor who is the fountain of them. For, since we are conscious that we have them, and yet have them not of ourselves, we must have them from some other.

对以上种种，我还须补上一句：这个词的用法有一种无从究诘的随意，而且它常常只是被当作一个词、仅此而已，用的人自己也不知道用它意指什么。222然而，无论取哪种含义，它都不能取代神性的存在。

十五、*生命、感觉、能动，以及我们自己心灵的诸官能，表明存在某个更高的存在者，它们皆由祂而来。*或者说，*上帝是这样的存在者：没有祂，这些东西便不能存在，正如前述的那些事物一样。*它们不可能从我们周围任何物质的本性——物质作为物质——流出，也不可能从它的任何样态、大小或运动流出；这一点即使现在还不明显，或可于后文更充分地证明。而我们灵魂自身并非自有永有、其诸官能并非独立于一切别的存在者，则由命题四与命题七得出。因此，我们在这方面所有的一切，必得感谢某位伟大的施予者，祂是这一切的源头。因为我们既意识到自己拥有它们，却又并非得自自己，就必是从某个别的存在者得来。

A man has little reason, God knows, to fancy the suppositum of his life, sense, and cogitative faculties to be an independent being, when he considers how transitory and uncertain at best his life and all his enjoyments are: what he is, whence he came, and whither he is going.223 The mind acts not, or in the most imperceptible manner, *in animalculo*, or the seminal state of a man; only as a principle of vegetation in the state of an embryon; and as a sensitive soul in the state of infancy, at least for some time, in which we are rather below than above many other animals. By degrees indeed, with age and exercise and proper opportunities, it seems to open itself, find its own talents, and ripen into a rational being. But then it reasons not without labor, and is forced to take many tedious steps in the pursuit of truth; finds all its powers subject to great eclipses and diminutions, in the time of sleep, indisposition, sickness, etc., and at best reaching but a few objects in respect of all that are in the immensity of the universe; and, lastly, is obnoxious to many painful sensations and reflections. Had the soul of man the principle of its own existence and faculties within itself, clear of all dependence, it could not be liable to all these limitations and defects, to all these alterations and removes from one state to another: it must certainly be constant to itself, and persist in a uniform manner of being.

===Chinese===

一个人，老天知道，没有什么理由把自己生命、感觉与思维官能的那个主体设想为独立的存在者——只要他想想自己一生至多何等短暂无常、他的一切享用何等飘忽：他是什么、从何而来、又往何处去。223心灵在*animalculo*（人的种子状态）中不活动、或以最不可察的方式活动；在胚胎状态中只像一个生长的原则；在婴孩状态中——至少有一段时间——只是一颗感觉的灵魂，那时我们比起许多别的动物，毋宁说在其下而非在其上。诚然，随着年岁、操练与适当的机会，它仿佛渐次开放，发现自己的才具，成熟为一个理性的存在者。但它推理得费力气，追求真理须跨许多沉闷的步骤；它的一切能力在睡眠、失调、疾病等时刻都遭大幅的亏蚀；至多也只能触及浩瀚宇宙中无数对象里的寥寥几个；最后，还难免许多痛苦的感受与反思。人的灵魂倘若自身之内就有其存在与官能的原理、摆脱一切依赖，就不可能有这一切限制与缺陷、这一切状态的迁转改变：它必恒守自身、以齐一的方式存在。

===Original===

There may be, perhaps, who will say, that the soul, together with life, sense, etc., are propagated by traduction from parents to children, from them to their children again, and so from eternity,224 and that therefore nothing can be collected from the nature of them as to the existence of a Deity. Answer: if there could be such a traduction, yet to suppose one traduced to come from another traduced, and so *ab aeterno*, without any further account of the original of mankind, or taking in any author of this traductive power, is the same as to suppose an infinite series of moveds without a mover, or of effects without a cause, the absurdity of which is shown already, proposition I. But concerning this matter, I cannot but think further, after the following manner: What is meant by *tradux animae* ought to be clearly explained, for it is not easy to conceive how thought, or thinking substances, can be propagated after the manner of branches, or in any manner that can be analogous to it, or even warrant a metaphorical use of that phrase.225 It should also be told whether this traduction be made from one or from both the parents. If from one, from which of them is it? And if from both, then the same *tradux*, or branch, must always proceed from two stocks, which is a thing, I presume, that can nowhere else be found, nor has any parallel in nature. And yet such a thing may much better be supposed of vines, or plants, than of thinking beings, who are simple and uncompounded substances.226

This opinion of the traduction of souls seems to me to stand upon an unsound foundation. For I take it to be grounded chiefly on these two things: the similitude there is between the features, humors, and abilities of children and those of their parents;227 and the difficulty men find in forming the notion of a spirit.228 For, from hence, they are apt to conclude that there can be no other substance but matter, and that the soul, resulting from some disposition of the body, or some part of it, or being some merely material appendix to it, must *attend* it, and come along with it from the parent or parents; and as there is a derivation of the one, so there must be also of the other at the same time.

===Chinese===

或许有人会说：灵魂连同生命、感觉等等，是由父母传递（traduction）给儿女，再由他们传给他们的儿女，如此自永恒以来代代相传，224因此从它们的本性推不出什么神性的存在。回答：即便能有这样的传递，设想一个被传递者出自另一个被传递者、如此*自永恒*（ab aeterno），而对人类的起源不作任何进一步的交代、也不引入这传递之力的任何赋予者，就同设想一串没有推动者的被推动者、或没有原因的结果一样，其荒谬已见于命题一。而关于此事，我不能不作进一步的思考如下：*tradux animae*（灵魂的传递）究竟何指，应当讲清楚；因为很难设想思想、或思维实体，能像枝条那样传递，或以任何可与之类比的方式传递，甚至很难说这个比喻说法有什么根据。225还应当说明：这传递是出自父母一方还是双方。若是一方，出自哪一方？若是双方，那么同一根*枝条*就必总是从两个树干里长出来——这样的事，我料想在别处任何地方都找不到，在自然中也没有平行的例子。况且这样的事设想在葡萄藤或植物上，还比设想在思维者身上好得多——思维者乃是单纯而不复合的实体。226

灵魂传递之说，在我看来立足不稳。因为我认为它主要建立在两件事上：子女与父母在相貌、性情与才能上的相似；227以及人们在形成精神实体观念上的困难。228因为由此他们便易于断言：除了物质不可能有别的实体，灵魂既由身体的某种配置、或其某部分产生、或只是它的一个纯物质附庸，就必*伴随*它、随它一同出自父母；一者有传承，另一者也就必同时有传承。
